MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
Here's everything. The route works, but only just, so read the timing note.

## Route and timeline

**Order: B, then A, then C.** It's the only order that works. A and B both need the morning, and B has to finish before 09:30, so A can't come first. C can't take anything before 11:00, so it has to be last.

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at B, unload |
| 09:05 | Leave B (done 25 min before the 09:30 opening) |
| 09:30 | Arrive at A, unload (within the 09:00–10:00 window) |
| 09:45 | Leave A |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C. **30-minute break, 10:25–10:55** |
| 11:00 | Unload at C |
| 11:15 | Leave C |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** |

**The catch: the return has no slack at all.** Any order has to finish at C, which can't start before 11:00. With 15 minutes to unload and 45 minutes back, the earliest possible return is exactly 12:00. That also assumes the drive back from C takes the same 45 minutes as the drive out, which you'll want to check.

The morning is fine. B has 25 minutes of slack, A has 15, and the wait before C absorbs any earlier delays. But if C is late letting him in, or there's traffic on the way back, he'll be past 12:00. Before tomorrow, it's worth doing one of these:
- **Check whether "back by 12:00" can stretch** by 15–30 minutes.
- **Ask C if they can be ready at exactly 11:00**, so he isn't kept waiting.
- **Move C to another day** if 12:00 is a hard limit.

## Van name ideas

- **Chippendale**
- **Dovetail**
- **The Sheraton**
- **Veneer There, Done That**

The first three are names of classic furniture makers and joints, which suits a restorer.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Condition:** look over every surface for new scratches, dents or chips. If you have photos from collection, compare against those.
2. **Completeness:** make sure every part is there and it's the right item. That includes shelves, glass, keys, handles, feet and fixings.
3. **Function:** open drawers and doors, and check legs and joints are firm and nothing has come loose in transit.

Then ask the customer to look it over before they sign.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed**, with the customer signing on the driver's phone. It's timestamped, harder to lose, and easy to find if there's ever a dispute. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who don't have email or prefer paper.

## Proof of delivery, in a line

> **Proof of delivery:** a signed record, usually with the customer's name, the date and time, and often a photo, showing the item was handed over and in what condition.

## Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Company] is due tomorrow between [time]. Reply here if that doesn't suit. Thanks!

The fixed wording is 92 characters, which leaves 68 for the name, company and time window. A typical message comes to about 130–140 characters.

When you set it up, use a plain straight apostrophe (') in "doesn't" and a plain hyphen in times like "9:00-10:00." Curly apostrophes, the long dashes some phones insert automatically, and emoji can switch the text to a different encoding. That cuts the single-message limit from 160 characters to 70, so the text would be sent as several messages.
